meta.title: Development Law Docket
meta.what_this_is: Indian court judgments that changed what development organisations, state programmes and rights-holders can actually do.
meta.what_this_is_not: Legal advice. Holdings are summarised editorially; the linked judgment is authoritative. Case law changes, so check the status field and the date.
meta.verification: Every entry's case name and decision year were checked against the judgment text, and each entry lists the specific terms confirmed present in that text. Summaries of what a case means are editorial and were not separately adjudicated.

judgments.case: Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa
judgments.holding: The Court set aside the termination of a Goa University employee after a complaints committee inquiry that fell short of natural justice, and remanded the inquiry to the committee with a three-month limit. In the same judgment it directed the Union, the States and the Union Territories to carry out a time-bound exercise to verify that ministries, departments, public authorities, statutory professional bodies, universities, colleges and government and private hospitals have constituted Internal, Local or Internal Complaints Committees as the PoSH Act requires, and to file compliance affidavits within eight weeks. The committee details must be published on each body's website.
judgments.what_changed: The directions bind the Union, the States and the Union Territories to verify that the listed bodies have constituted committees as the PoSH Act requires and to report by affidavit, and each body must publish its committee's composition and contact details on its website. The Court recorded that committees found in place often lacked the mandatory external member. On 10 February 2026 it was still taking States' compliance affidavits and listed the matter for 17 March 2026.

judgments.case: Deepika Singh v. Central Administrative Tribunal
judgments.holding: The Court held that a PGIMER employee with one biological child, who had been given child care leave for her husband's two children from an earlier marriage, was entitled to maternity leave under Rule 43 of the Central Civil Services (Leave) Rules 1972. It said the child care leave she had taken could not be used to deny her maternity leave. In the same judgment the Court observed that atypical families, including single-parent households, unmarried partnerships and queer relationships, deserve protection under social welfare legislation.
judgments.what_changed: The decision concerns Rule 43 of the Central Civil Services (Leave) Rules 1972 and a government employee. The remarks on atypical families are observations and lay down no rule for other employers or programmes.

judgments.case: Noel Harper v. Union of India
judgments.holding: The Court held Sections 7, 12(1A), 12A and 17 of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act 2010, as amended in 2020, to be within the Constitution. Amended Section 7 bars a registered person from transferring foreign contribution to any other person, and Sections 12(1A) and 17 require foreign contribution to be received in an FCRA account at the SBI New Delhi Main Branch. The Court read down Section 12A so that Indian office bearers may produce an Indian passport for identification, which counts as compliance.
judgments.what_changed: Section 7 as amended bars transfer of foreign contribution to any other person, including a person holding a registration certificate, so a registered organisation must use the amount itself. Foreign contribution must be received in the FCRA account at the SBI New Delhi Main Branch under Sections 12(1A) and 17.

judgments.case: X v. Principal Secretary, Health & Family Welfare, NCT of Delhi
judgments.holding: The Court read Rule 3B(c) of the Medical Termination of Pregnancy Rules to include unmarried and single women, so that they can seek termination between 20 and 24 weeks on the same footing as married women. It held that rape in Rule 3B(a) includes marital rape for the purposes of the MTP Act only, and left the validity of Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC to other proceedings. It also held that a registered medical practitioner, on request of a minor and her guardian, need not disclose the minor's identity when reporting under Section 19(1) of the POCSO Act.
judgments.what_changed: Marital status does not decide access to termination between 20 and 24 weeks under Rule 3B. A woman who says her pregnancy resulted from rape by her husband can rely on Rule 3B(a), and the Court said no FIR or proof of the allegation in court is required for the purposes of the MTP Act. The Court left the constitutional validity of the marital rape exception in the criminal law to other proceedings.

judgments.case: State of Kerala v. Leesamma Joseph
judgments.holding: Under the Persons with Disabilities Act 1995, a person with benchmark disability is entitled to be considered for reservation in promotion in posts identified for persons with disabilities, even where the service rules provide no such reservation and even where the employee did not enter service through the disability quota. The Court dismissed Kerala's appeal and directed the State to identify the posts and provide reservation in promotion within three months.
judgments.what_changed: The route of entry into service does not decide eligibility. What counts is that the employee has the disability when promotion is considered. The Court noted that the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 now deals with reservation in promotion.

judgments.case: Vikash Kumar v. Union Public Service Commission
judgments.holding: The Court held that the appellant, who has writer's cramp, a chronic neurological condition listed in the Schedule to the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act 2016 but below the 40% benchmark, is entitled to a scribe for the Civil Services Examination and any other competitive selection conducted under government authority. It held that reasonable accommodation is an individualised duty and that a person should not be expected to be 'disabled enough' to claim it. It directed the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment to frame scribe guidelines in consultation with persons with disabilities within three months.
judgments.what_changed: A candidate with a specified disability under Section 2(s) of the 2016 Act who falls short of benchmark disability can claim a scribe for the Civil Services Examination and other competitive selections under government authority. The Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment issued Office Memorandum F.No.29-6/2019-DD-III on 10 August 2022. In Gulshan Kumar v Institute of Banking Personnel Selection (3 February 2025, 2025 INSC 142) the Court directed the Ministry to revisit that memorandum, remove the restrictions and re-notify it within two months, so that scribe and compensatory time reach all candidates with disabilities.

judgments.case: Alembic Pharmaceuticals v. Rohit Prajapati
judgments.holding: The Court held that an ex post facto environmental clearance is contrary to the EIA Notification of 27 January 1994 and that the Ministry's circular of 14 May 2002 allowing it is unsustainable in law. It set aside the NGT's direction to revoke the clearances and close three industrial units, and instead directed each of the three units to deposit ₹10 crore as compensation with the Gujarat Pollution Control Board within four months, under Article 142.
judgments.what_changed: Alembic did not order closure, citing proportionality, and imposed compensation instead. Vanashakti v Union of India (29 July 2026, 2026 INSC 761) now governs the question: it held that the prior clearance regime under the 2006 Notification is mandatory, and that the Alembic observations on ex post facto clearance must be read in their statutory context and do not bar the Central Government from issuing a narrowly tailored amnesty notification. It upheld the 2017 Notification and quashed the 2021 Office Memorandum with prospective effect.

judgments.case: Secretary, Ministry of Defence v. Babita Puniya
judgments.holding: The Court accepted the Union's policy of 25 February 2019 and directed that permanent commission be considered for all serving women Short Service Commission officers in the Army's ten streams, irrespective of having crossed fourteen or twenty years of service, with the same choice of specialisation as men. It held that the 'staff appointments only' limit in that policy shall not be enforced. It rejected the Union's arguments based on physiology, motherhood and unit dynamics as sex stereotypes that discriminate against women.
judgments.what_changed: Blanket non-consideration of women for command appointments, without an individuated justification by the Army, cannot be sustained in law. The Court added that whether women officers should hold particular command assignments is a matter for the relevant authority. Its reasoning on stereotypes answers the Army's own arguments.

judgments.case: Indian Social Action Forum (INSAF) v. Union of India
judgments.holding: The Court read down Rules 3(v) and 3(vi) of the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Rules 2011, which list grounds for declaring an organisation to be of a political nature. It held that 'political interests' in Rule 3(v), and habitual use of bandh, hartal and similar methods in Rule 3(vi), apply only to organisations connected with active politics or party politics. It left the Central Government free to act against organisations used to channel foreign funds for political parties where it has concrete material and follows the procedure in the Act and Rules.
judgments.what_changed: Supporting a public cause by lawful protest, or working for social and economic welfare, does not make an organisation one of a political nature under Rule 3(v) or 3(vi). The Court tied both rules to a connection with active or party politics. An organisation facing a declaration under Section 5 can rely on this reading.

judgments.case: In Re: Problems and Miseries of Migrant Labourers
judgments.holding: In suo motu proceedings on migrant workers during the COVID-19 lockdown, the order of 9 June 2020 directed States and Union Territories to transport all stranded workers by train, bus or other mode within 15 days. It declined to direct direct bank transfers.

The Court had reviewed the working of the Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act 1979, which has since been subsumed in the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code 2020; the four labour codes took effect on 21 November 2025.

judgments.case: CPIO, Supreme Court of India v. Subhash Chandra Agarwal
judgments.holding: A five-judge Bench held that the Supreme Court of India, which includes the office of the Chief Justice, is a public authority under the RTI Act. It held that the fiduciary relationship exemption in Section 8(1)(e) does not apply to judges' asset declarations, and that where the contents of declarations are sought the public interest test under Section 8(1)(j) and the proviso to Section 11(1) applies. It partly allowed the two other appeals and remitted them to the CPIO to decide after notice to third parties, and said independence of the judiciary is a matter of public interest.
judgments.what_changed: A request to the Supreme Court registry for information on judges' asset declarations is dealt with under the RTI Act, with notice to third parties where Section 11(1) applies. Section 44(3) of the Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 substituted Section 8(1)(j) of the RTI Act with "information which relates to personal information;", and came into force on 13 November 2025. The substituted clause does not contain the public interest test that this judgment applied under Section 8(1)(j).

judgments.case: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
judgments.holding: A five-judge Bench struck down Section 497 IPC (adultery) as violative of Articles 14, 15 and 21, and held Section 198(2) CrPC unconstitutional insofar as it applied to the offence under Section 497. On 31 January 2023 a five-judge Bench clarified that the 2018 judgment did not pronounce on the Army Act, the Navy Act or the Air Force Act.

judgments.case: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Aadhaar)
judgments.holding: On 26 September 2018 a five-judge Constitution Bench upheld the Aadhaar Act, 2016 by majority, holding it validly passed as a Money Bill and Section 7 valid; Chandrachud J dissented and held the Act unconstitutional for having been passed as a Money Bill. The majority struck down Section 33(2) in its present form and the part of Section 57 that let body corporates and individuals seek authentication under a contract, quashed the Department of Telecommunications circular of 23 March 2017 on mobile linking, held Rule 9 of the PMLA Rules disproportionate as to bank accounts, and found Section 139AA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 to satisfy the privacy tests.
judgments.what_changed: CBSE, NEET, JEE and UGC cannot make Aadhaar mandatory, because they are outside Section 7 and not backed by any law, and school admission cannot require it. Enrolling a child needs the consent of a parent or guardian, and the Court took on record the Attorney General's statement that no deserving person would be denied a scheme's benefit on the failure of authentication. The Aadhaar and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019 later substituted new sub-sections (3) to (7) in Section 4 of the Aadhaar Act, providing for voluntary use of Aadhaar by authentication or offline verification, and Section 4(7) makes authentication mandatory where a law made by Parliament requires it.
judgments.status_note: The Money Bill part of the holding was doubted in Rojer Mathew v. South Indian Bank (2019), which referred the Money Bill question to a larger bench. The review petitions against the 2018 judgment were dismissed on 11 January 2021, Chandrachud J dissenting.

judgments.holding: On 9 February 2018 the Supreme Court gave sixteen directions on implementing the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, and disposed of the petition. They include that State Governments must fill Juvenile Justice Board and Child Welfare Committee positions expeditiously, that those bodies must sit regularly, that NCPCR and the State commissions must study how many Probation Officers are needed so that States can appoint them, and that Special Juvenile Police Units must be set up at the earliest as meaningful working units. The Court asked the Chief Justice of each High Court to register a case on its own motion on implementation, and directed the Registry to list the matter on 13 March 2018 for directions after the High Courts' responses.

Other directions are phrased as advice, such as registering Child Care Institutions and appointing civil society Visitors ('would be well advised'), and carry less force than the 'must' directions. The judgment can be cited when pressing a State to staff these bodies.

judgments.case: Independent Thought v. Union of India
judgments.holding: On 11 October 2017 the Supreme Court read down Exception 2 to Section 375 IPC so that sexual intercourse or sexual acts by a man with his own wife, the wife not being under eighteen years of age, is not rape. Sexual intercourse with a wife aged 15 to 18 is therefore rape. Gupta J, in a separate concurring judgment, added that the judgment has prospective effect, and the Court left the marital rape of adult women undecided.

The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which repealed the IPC and came into force on 1 July 2024, carries the age of eighteen in Exception 2 to its Section 63.

judgments.case: K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (Privacy)
judgments.holding: On 24 August 2017 a nine-judge Constitution Bench held that privacy is a constitutionally protected right, intrinsic to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III. It overruled M P Sharma to the extent it indicated otherwise and overruled the second part of Kharak Singh, which held that privacy is not a guaranteed right. In the plurality opinion of Chandrachud J, an invasion of life or personal liberty must meet a three-fold requirement of legality, a legitimate state aim and proportionality.
judgments.what_changed: A state measure that collects or uses personal information has to be justified against those three requirements, and the Aadhaar judgment of 26 September 2018 tested the Aadhaar Act against them. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 is the statute on the processing of digital personal data, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025 were notified on 13 November 2025 with most rules, including rules 3 and 5 to 16, coming into force eighteen months after publication.

judgments.holding: On 15 December 2017 the Supreme Court gave eleven directions on accessibility under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 and listed the matter for directions after three months, so the petition was not disposed of. judgments.case: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
judgments.holding: On 22 August 2017 a five-judge Constitution Bench set aside talaq-e-biddat (instant triple talaq) by a majority of 3:2. Nariman and Lalit JJ declared Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937 void to the extent it recognises and enforces triple talaq, because that form of talaq is manifestly arbitrary under Article 14. Kurian Joseph J held it contrary to the basic tenets of the Quran. Khehar CJ and Nazeer J, in the minority, directed the Union to consider legislation and injuncted Muslim husbands from pronouncing it for six months in the first instance.
judgments.what_changed: An instant triple talaq does not end a Muslim marriage. The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 defines 'talaq' as talaq-e-biddat or any similar form having the effect of instantaneous and irrevocable divorce, declares any such pronouncement void and illegal (section 3), and punishes the husband with imprisonment of up to three years and a fine (section 4). A woman on whom talaq is pronounced is entitled to subsistence allowance and custody of minor children as the Magistrate determines (sections 5 and 6).
judgments.status_note: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 declares a pronouncement of talaq-e-biddat void and illegal and makes it an offence punishable with up to three years' imprisonment and a fine.

judgments.case: Swaraj Abhiyan v. Union of India
judgments.holding: On 11 May 2016 the Supreme Court held that a declaration of drought is not a judicially manageable exercise and no judicially acceptable standards can be laid down for declaring or not declaring one, while saying the judiciary cannot take a hands-off approach and may issue directions under Article 21. It directed that the Drought Management Manual be revised and updated on or before 31 December 2016, with a mandated time limit for declaring a drought. On 13 May 2016 it directed the States before it to appoint District Grievance Redressal Officers and constitute State Food Commissions under the National Food Security Act, to give every household in a drought-affected area its monthly entitlement of food grains regardless of a ration card, to provide eggs, milk or a nutritional substitute under the Mid-Day Meal Scheme and extend that Scheme through the summer vacation, and directed the Government of India to see that compensation is paid to workers whose wages were delayed beyond 15 days under the National Rural Employment Guarantee Act.
judgments.what_changed: The Court did not set standards for declaring a drought. It ordered a revised Manual with a time limit and directed the Secretary in the Union Department of Agriculture to meet the Chief Secretaries of Bihar, Gujarat and Haryana within a week and, if so advised, persuade the State Government to declare a drought in whichever district, taluka, tehsil or block is necessary. A household in a drought-affected area cannot be denied its National Food Security Act grains only because it has no ration card. The MGNREGA directions now concern a repealed Act: a PIB note of 11 May 2026 states that the Viksit Bharat Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 comes into force with effect from 1 July 2026, as notified, and that Mahatma Gandhi NREGA stands repealed from that date.

judgments.case: Laxmi v. Union of India
judgments.holding: In Laxmi v. Union of India (judgment of 18 July 2013, reported at (2014) 4 SCC 427) the Supreme Court prohibited over-the-counter sale of acid unless the seller keeps a register and the buyer shows a government photo ID with address and states the purpose, and barred sale to anyone under 18, until State rules in line with the Centre's Model Rules are operational. The District Legal Services Authority, with the District Judge and co-opted officers, functions as the Criminal Injuries Compensation Board for these claims.
